final_proof:
Let \(\langle P,s,0\rangle\) be a Peano structure. Thus \(0\in P\), the successor map is a map \(s:P\to P\), \(0\notin s[P]\), and the induction axiom holds: if \(A\subseteq P\), \(0\in A\), and \(s[A]\subseteq A\), then \(A=P\). (The injectivity axiom for \(s\), though part of the usual definition, is not needed here.)

Define \(A=s[P]\cup\{0\}\). Because \(s:P\to P\) and \(0\in P\), we have \(A\subseteq P\). Clearly \(0\in A\). Moreover, if \(a\in A\), then \(a\in P\), so \(s(a)\in s[P]\subseteq A\). Hence \(s[A]\subseteq A\). The induction axiom therefore gives
\[
P=A=s[P]\cup\{0\}.
\]

It remains to compute the indicated set difference. The Peano axiom \(0\notin s[P]\) shows that \(0\in P\setminus s[P]\). Conversely, if \(x\in P\setminus s[P]\), then \(x\in P=s[P]\cup\{0\}\); since \(x\notin s[P]\), it follows that \(x=0\). Consequently
\[
P\setminus s[P]=\{0\},
\]
which is a singleton. Thus \(0\) is the unique non-successor element of \(P\).
